ruling_text:
Barry Hosier v. Camino Ramon Terrace Owner's Association

Camino Ramon Terrace Owner’s Association’s Motion to Compel is GRANTED. The
deposition of M3 Construction General Contractor, Inc.’s Person Most Knowledgeable is
to take place on or before April 24, 2026. The Association’s request for sanctions is
GRANTED, however, the amount requested is unreasonable and is reduced to $860. 2
hours of work at $400 per hour, plus $60 filing fee. M3 is to pay sanctions in the amount
of $860 by April 24, 2026.

California Code of Civil Procedure (C.C.P.) section 2025.220 does not state that a party
seeking to depose an individual cannot do so “unilaterally.” In fact, the statute expressly
requires that a date be set and noticed. (Id. subd. (a)(2).) While this court observes that it
would be reasonable and more efficient for one side to reach out to the other in advance to
work out dates, the statute does not require such and M3 Construction General Contractor,
Inc’s objection to the noticed depositions as being “unilaterally set” is without merit. (See
Code Civ. Proc., §§ 2025.210-2025.295.) The court also observes that counsel for the Camino
Ramon Terrace Owner’s Association (“the Association”) sent an email to M3’s counsel on
August 27, 2025 and September 15, 2025 (as to the first notice) and again on September 19,
2025 with a formal letter on September 29, 2025 (as to the second notice) in an effort to obtain
dates for the depositions which were met without success.
It appears by M3’s own admission they did not provide dates for the deposition of their person
most knowledgeable until March 12, 2026, seven months after the Association’s first request
for dates, four months after the November 17, 2025, filing of the Association’s motion to
compel and just 14 days before the hearing on the motion. The Association has been seeking
dates for this deposition since August 2025. This court reviewed M3’s explanation for the
delay and while this court is quite sympathetic to the stress and distrust that one may feel when
faced with the unfamiliarity of our court processes, this is a sentiment often shared by
individuals that appear in litigation as a party or even witnesses. While an explanation for the
circumstances, it is not an excuse. Mr. Musser’s hesitation and concerns are understandable,
but it is not an excuse for counsel to fail to be able to obtain a single date between August
2025 and March 2026 for Mr. Musser to appear. The court would further observe that the
emails that were provided to the court by M3 in support of their Opposition suggest an offer
by Mr. Musser to provide more accommodating weekday dates for his deposition should the
Association dismiss this motion and request for sanctions. This appears to demonstrate some
knowledge or understanding on the part of Mr. Musser as to what was at stake related to this
motion.

Of note, this court does not find that either party’s efforts to meet and confer were meaningful
and focused on working out their differences.
“The Discovery Act requires that, prior to the initiation of a motion to compel, the moving
party declare that he or she has made a serious attempt to obtain ‘an informal resolution of
each issue.’ [Citations.] This rule is designed ‘to encourage the parties to work out their
differences informally so as to avoid the necessity for a formal order. …’ [Citation.] This, in
turn, will lessen the burden on the court and reduce the unnecessary expenditure of resources
by litigants through promotion of informal, extrajudicial resolution of discovery disputes.
[Citations.]” (Townsend v. Superior Court (1998) 61 Cal. App. 4th 1431, 1435.) “[W]e find
that the statute requires that there be a serious effort at negotiation and informal resolution. We
leave it to the parties to determine the proper time, manner, and place for such discussion.”
(Townsend, supra, p. 1438.)
While counsel for the Association made efforts to communicate and obtain dates through
email, some of which were responded to by M3’s counsel, and a formal letter, at no time did
either parties’ counsel attempt to call one another or meet in person to work things out. (See
California Rules of Court Rule 3.724, Contra Costa County Local Rule 2.121, subd. (e).) Meet
and confer efforts require more than futile emails and a one-sided formal letter. (See C.C.P.,
§§ 2016.040; 2019.030, subd. (b), 2030.090, subd. (a), 2031.060, subd (a).)
Nonetheless, the Court finds that M3 failed to provide dates for deposition of their person
most knowledgeable prior to March 12, 2026; many of the dates provided were weekend
dates; and all dates appear to not be available for the Association. Given the seven-month
delay and limited weekday dates provided, the court does not find the motion to compel now
moot, rather, the motion to compel is GRANTED. The deposition of M3 Construction
General Contractor, Inc.’s Person Most Knowledgeable is to take place on or before
April 24, 2026.
“If, after service of a deposition notice…without having served a valid objection…[the person]
fails to appear for examination…the party giving the notice may move for an order compelling
…attendance and testimony…If a motion under subdivision (a) is granted, the court shall
impose a monetary sanction…in favor of the party who noticed the deposition and against the
deponent or the party with whom the deponent is affiliated, unless the court finds that the one
subject to the sanction acted with substantial justification or that other circumstances make the
imposition of the sanction unjust.” (C.C.P. §2025.450, subd. (a)&(g).) “‘[T]he phrase
“substantial justification” has been understood to mean that a justification is clearly reasonable
because it is well grounded in both law and fact.’” (Kwan Software Engineering, Inc., supra,
p. 75, citing Doe v. U.S. Swimming, Inc. (2011) 200 Cal.App.4th 1424, 1434.) “If the party
seeking a monetary sanction meets its burden of proof, the burden shifts to the opposing party
attempting to avoid a monetary sanction to show that it acted with ‘substantial justification.’”
(U.S. Swimming, Inc., supra, p. 1435.)
“The trial court has broad discretion in deciding whether to impose sanctions and in setting the
amount of monetary sanctions.” (Cornerstone Realty Advisors, LLC v. Summit Healthcare
Reit, Inc. (2020) 56 Cal.App.5th 771, 789.)
As previously stated, M3’s objection to the deposition was not valid and the court does not
find that M3’s conduct was with substantial justification. Sanctions are appropriate for the
seven-month delay in providing dates for the deposition and failing to produce Mr. Musser at
the two dates noticed. (See C.C.P. §2025.450 (g)(2).) The Association’s request for
sanctions is GRANTED, however, the amount requested is unreasonable and is reduced.
2 hours of work at $400 per hour, plus $60 filing fee. M3 is to pay sanctions in the
amount of $860 by April 24, 2026.
